21.0.s.en: (1) The war with the king of Arad

21.0.0.en: Canaanite: that is, from the descendants of Canaan, son of Noah's son Ham, but the curse came upon him, so the Canaanites did not walk in God's statutes but became an example of evil.

21.0.1.en: Arad: a Canaanite city in the south of Palestine.

21.0.2.en: The south: what is meant is the south of Palestine.

21.0.3.en: The way of the spies: this is the road that the twelve spies had taken before to enter the land. The Canaanite king of the town of Arad heard of the matter of the people and that their aim was to pass through, and learned of their talk with the Edomites and the refusal of the king of the Edomites to let them pass (ch. 20). Because of this king's abundant evil, he attacked the peaceful people and took some of them as captives to be slaves for his people. Perhaps Arad's attack on the children of Israel was out of fear of their great number, so he rushed to attack them and took some of them captive to frighten them so that they would keep away from him (maps 2, 4).

21.1.0.en: The people took refuge in God, their leader and supreme governor, and prayed to Him, and vowed a vow to God that if He gave them victory over this wicked king and their captive brothers were freed, they would utterly destroy the cities of Arad, that is, destroy and wipe out the buildings of the city.

21.2.0.en: We see God's just answer, for He permitted His people this war and also gave them victory.

21.2.1.en: The expression "delivered up the Canaanites" means that God handed the enemies over to the people to do with them as they wished, and that the victory was fundamentally from the Lord and not by the hand of Israel. Indeed the people destroyed everything, and therefore the place was afterward called "Hormah," as a sign and allusion to what happened there.

21.2.2.en: May we not let our feelings or emotions lead us to act in any situation, but let us bring all our complaints and feelings to God in prayer, trusting and believing that God is able to solve all our problems or to guide us to what we ought to do.

21.3.0.en: When the king of Edom refused to let the people pass, Moses was compelled to go around the land of Edom, so they passed by Elath, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, then eastward at Mount "Hor," which lies south of Palestine and east of the Gulf of Aqaba, a difficult mountain road, which had a bad effect on the morale of the people, who became very discouraged.

21.4.0.en: In a new episode in the series of murmurings of the people of the children of Israel in the Book of Numbers, the people expressed their anger with words very wounding to the heart of God, for they murmured against God Himself and against Moses their leader, forgetting all God's earlier works of care and providence. Their murmuring included three things:

21.4.1.en: 1- Their coming out of the land of Egypt, forgetting their former bondage and forced labor.

21.4.2.en: 2- Complaining of the lack of water and bread, although God daily undertook to feed them.

21.4.3.en: 3- Describing the "manna," the free divine food, as light bread, in clear contempt for the love and gift of God.

21.5.1.en: God's punishment of this ungrateful people was clear and severe, so He sent among them serpents whose bites were highly poisonous and very painful, and many of the people died as a result. It is to be noted that God had kept His people on their way from the fiery serpents hiding in the mountains, but when they murmured against Him they lost His protection, so the serpents attacked them and bit them and they died.

21.6.0.en: The scene is repeated, and Israel feels its error and that it had gone beyond every limit when it insulted its God. They confessed before Moses and God the greatness of the offense of their error and asked Moses for intercessory prayer on their behalf so that God would remove from them the punishment of the serpents. And because Moses was a loving shepherd and an intercessor beloved of God, he indeed lifted up his prayers to God for his people.

21.7.0.en: God intervened at once and answered the prayer of Moses and commanded him to make a serpent of bronze in the form of the fiery serpents that were biting the people, and to lift it up on a pole or a high column like a banner, so that everyone bitten by one of the serpents might see it and be saved from the poison by looking at this bronze serpent.

21.7.1.en: It is to be noted that the serpent made of bronze cannot heal from deadly poison, but God wanted to test the obedience of His people and their faith by their looking at this bronze serpent, and He healed them because He is the Healer, and He asks only obedience and faith from His children.

21.7.2.en: My beloved brother .. if you feel that you have sinned and that God in His love has allowed you to be disciplined, return at once with repentance and confession of your error, and ask the prayer of your father the priest at the altar, and God will answer you and remove His wrath from you.

21.8.0.en: Moses did as the Lord commanded him and set the bronze serpent on a raised pole and a high place, so that whenever any person bitten by a poisonous serpent looked at it with hope and faith, God healed him and he escaped death. The spiritual meanings in this lifted-up serpent are many, but the most important thing in this story is the very clear symbol between the lifted-up serpent and Christ, who was also lifted up on the wood of the Cross, and here, beloved, are some aspects of this likeness:

21.8.1.en: 1- The serpents bit the people and they died, as the ancient serpent brought down Adam and he was sentenced to death.

21.8.2.en: 2- The people cried out to God for deliverance, as humanity cried out for redemption from the sentence of death.

21.8.3.en: 3- Moses made a likeness of the same kind, that is, a bronze serpent like the serpents, and thus God took a body like our bodies, but it did not carry poison (sin) but deliverance and life.

21.8.4.en: 4- Moses lifted the bronze serpent high, and Christ was also lifted up on the Cross so that everyone who believes in Him might be saved from the bites of Satan and sin and have eternal life.

21.8.5.en: Sadly, when the people grew weak in their relationship with God, they worshiped the bronze serpent as they had worshiped the statues of the pagan gods, and they called the image of the serpent "Nehushtan," and therefore Hezekiah king of Judah crushed it to remove this pagan worship (2 Kgs 18:4).

21.8.6.en: Let us lift up our eyes in faith toward the Cross, seeking healing from our sins, remembering that He who went up on the Cross opened His arms and His bosom to hold us within it, if we ourselves wish it.

21.9.1.en: The people journeyed to Oboth, and from Oboth northward to Ije-abarim, which has another name, "Iim," by which it is mentioned in ch. (33:45). The expression "before Moab, toward the sunrising" means east of Moab (map 3).

21.10.0.en: The journey continued to a valley named "Zared," which took its name from a small river of the same name, "Zared," a river that flows into the Dead Sea and is considered the dividing boundary between Edom to the south and the land of Moab to the north.

21.11.0.en: Israel also journeyed northward to a new river, the river "Arnon," which represents a new boundary between Moab to the south and the Amorites to the north. The expression in the wilderness "that cometh out of the coasts of the Amorites" means that this journeying was alongside the land of the Amorites, that is, the river Arnon was between the people and the Amorites.

21.12.0.en: The book of the wars of the Lord: this is a historical book from the books of the people, written by Moses, and it is a record of God's work in the confrontations, wars and situations that the people met on their way and journeying. It is a historical book and not among the holy inspired Scriptures.

21.12.1.en: Suphah: the region around the Red Sea.

21.12.2.en: The brooks: the slope of the valley of Arnon.

21.12.3.en: Ar: the capital of the land of Moab.

21.12.5.en: Moses, "the writer of the Book of Numbers," matches the events of the journeying here and also confirms them by the fact that this was recorded in another book written in poetic form, describing the same events and places. And since the prophet Moses relied on the book of the wars of the Lord, this means that it was written before the Book of Numbers, and this book mentions that God was with His people Israel, and as He brought it through the Red Sea and gave it victory, so also He gave it victories at the river Arnon and it passed by the land of Moab.

21.13.0.en: The people journeyed again from the valley of Arnon, and when their weariness increased, the Lord guided them to a place to dig a well there: "Gather the people together, and I will give them water."

21.14.0.en: Because of the greatness of the Lord's work for the people, the children of Israel praised God with a new song, thanking Him by it for what He had done with them by helping them to dig this well through their princes, and He brought them through until they passed the borders of the land of Moab. The words of this song came as follows: Spring up, O well: rise up, O waters.

21.14.1.en: Sing ye unto it: sing and chant to it.

21.14.2.en: The well which the princes digged, the nobles of the people: that is, those who did the digging were those counted as princes and nobles of the people and not just any ordinary folk, in response to God's request.

21.14.3.en: By the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves: the scepter is the king's rod and symbolizes authority and majesty, and the staves symbolize hard work and striving, that is, the water came out by divine authority and the effort of the noble men. This meaning is very close to what the Church teaches, that salvation is in the first place a work of divine grace ("the scepter"), provided that man responds to grace through his spiritual striving ("the staves").

21.15.0.en: Mattanah: a city on the border of Moab.

21.15.1.en: In these two verses is a continuation of the people's journey and journeying, and it mentions a series of places they passed through from the south of the Dead Sea going north alongside it until they reached a place called "the top of Pisgah," which is the head of a mountain that looks out over and overlooks the wilderness and lies east of the Dead Sea. This mountain was also called Mount "Nebo," and it is the place from which Moses saw the Promised Land and on which he also died.

21.16.s.en: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

21.16.0.en: The Amorites: they are the descendants of Canaan the son of Ham the son of Noah, and their land was very wide east of the river Jordan.

21.16.1.en: The king's highway: the main public road within the kingdom.

21.16.2.en: As Moses did with the king of Edom (ch. 20) and asked his permission to pass through his land, so also he did here with Sihon king of the Amorites, and even repeated exactly what he had said before in the wording of the request, that they would not touch anything of the fruit of the land and would not take water from their wells, but all they wanted was permission to pass only, so that they might cross the border. Although this land of the Amorites is a land that God promised to Abraham as an inheritance for his people, Moses did not begin with war but resorted to peace, dialogue and asking permission.

21.17.0.en: Jahaz: a Moabite city (map 5). Border: boundary.

21.17.1.en: Ashtaroth ● Edrei ● Dibon ● valley of Zared. Map (5). Sihon king of the Amorites was not content with refusal, but in pride and a display of strength without justification, he went out with his army into the wilderness to meet the people of God at a place called Jahaz, and the two parties met and the Lord gave victory to His people, and Israel prevailed by the edge of the sword, and the people took possession of all the cities of the Amorites, whose borders were from the river Arnon to the south to the river Jabbok to the north, and to the west was the river Jordan. The northern river Jabbok separated the border of the Amorites from the border of the children of Ammon, whom the Book describes as strong.

21.18.0.en: Heshbon: the largest city of the Amorites and their capital.

21.18.1.en: Israel possessed the land, which was the first land considered fit for dwelling after the long journey in the wilderness, and they settled in the capital of the Amorites, "Heshbon," and all the small villages around it.

21.19.0.en: This verse presents an addition, namely that this land of the Moabites had been seized by Sihon from the former king of Moab, and he took all the land with all its borders. The meaning intended to be made clear here is that the usurper, however great his power, has a day of punishment laid up for him by God, and as He did to the one before, He does also to him, for often the recompense is from the same deed, and what a man sows, that he will reap.

21.20.0.en: They that speak in proverbs: that is, the composers of the songs or ballads that record history and its events. The people sang of this victory and it became for them a beloved song commemorating this victory, and it included verses (27-30), and its first part spoke of the victory of Sihon king of the Amorites over the Moabites, and its second half (v. 30) spoke of the victory of the people of God over Sihon ... The meanings of the words of this poem were as follows:

21.20.1.en: Come into Heshbon: come to Heshbon, which had belonged to the Moabites.

21.20.2.en: The city of Sihon: that is, which after the victory of Sihon became the possession of him and his people the Amorites. A fire is gone out of Heshbon: fire and flame, that is, severe wars and battles, which Sihon waged from Heshbon on the rest of the cities of the Moabites until he occupied them all. As examples of these cities the singers mentioned the name of the city "Ar," and also the heights of Arnon.

21.20.3.en: Moab's great city: "great" meaning large, and the meaning is the great Moabite city, which is the capital, that is, Heshbon. The lords of the high places of Arnon: this means the princes or priests of the idols in the valley of Arnon.

21.20.4.en: Woe to thee, Moab: destruction has come to you, O cities of the Moabites.

21.20.5.en: O people of Chemosh: the speech is also about the destruction of the Moabites and the end of their pagan god Chemosh, for all his followers became either fugitives from before Sihon or slaves of the Amorites and their king Sihon.

21.21.0.en: This verse is the last stanza of the poem, but it speaks of the victory of the people of God over Sihon and the Amorites, and its meaning is:

21.21.1.en: We have shot at them: that is, we struck them and hit them.

21.21.2.en: Heshbon even unto Dibon: we destroyed our enemies from Heshbon in the north to the town of Dibon in the south, and our victory reached all the cities and borders of the Amorites, such as Nophah toward Medeba.

21.22.0.en: After the end of this song, which the singers and then the people sang, the people dwelt in all the land of the Moabites, and this victory had the greatest effect in raising their morale and began a series of other victories (map 5).

21.22.1.en: Do not fear the attack of the wicked upon you, because God is able to protect you from them and even to punish them for your sake. Only hold fast to God and ask His help at all times.

21.23.s.en: (5) The victory over the king of Bashan

21.23.0.en: Jazer: one of the cities of the Amorites on the border of the Ammonites, and therefore it was a fortified and strong city.

21.23.1.en: The people did not take the fortified city of "Jazer" at first, but after a period of settling in Heshbon and its villages, Moses sent spies to the city of Jazer. We understand from the words that the people were able to take it and its villages also.

21.24.0.en: The people continued to advance northward alongside the eastern bank of the river Jordan, and the city of Bashan was in their way, and Moses did not think of storming it or fighting it, but the king of Bashan, perhaps because of his fear of what had happened to the Amorites, gathered his men of war to the city of "Edrei," the largest of their cities and their capital at that time, to meet Moses and fight him.

21.25.0.en: As for Moses, who did nothing without God's guidance or asking Him, the divine signal came to him to advance and not fear, for God informed him that he would triumph over Og king of Bashan, and that the people would possess all his land, as He had previously given him victory over Sihon and he possessed all his land.

21.26.0.en: Indeed Israel prevailed over Og and all his army and destroyed them completely and took possession of the land as the Lord had said.

21.26.1.en: None left him remaining: that is, none of his men escaped, but they all perished.

21.26.2.en: Consult God in all your decisions and do not undertake anything without His will, for if you submit your will to His will you will be successful in all the matters of your life.

21.26.3.en: The story of Balaam, an introduction: the next three chapters speak of the story of Balaam and his meeting with Balak king of the Moabites and his pronouncing blessing on the people instead of a curse.
